title: METR benchmark: Anthropic's model development pace has roughly doubled in a year
subtitle: An updated analysis from the Model Evaluation and Threat Research group shows Claude Opus 4.6 clearing a 14.5-hour time horizon on software tasks — with doubling times now near four months.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Model Evaluation and Threat Research group (METR) has updated its time-horizons benchmark, and Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 is at the frontier. METR's latest fit places the top model's 50-percent time horizon at roughly 14.5 hours of human-equivalent software work, with a wide confidence interval of six to ninety-eight hours. The underlying trend now shows a doubling time of about four months — half the seven-month figure METR first reported in early 2025.

Time horizon is the length of task, in human work-hours, that a model can complete at a given success rate. It is not the model's wall-clock runtime. A fourteen-hour horizon means Opus 4.6 can finish problems that would take a competent engineer most of a day — not that the model takes a day to answer. Doubling times that compress from seven months to four months imply the frontier is accelerating, not plateauing, at least on tasks the benchmark can still measure.

That last caveat matters. METR researchers have publicly flagged that their current software task suite is approaching saturation — the hardest problems in the set are being solved, so new measurements have very wide error bars. The group has said it is 'increasingly nervous' about the precision of the numbers, even as the directional story holds. Anthropic itself has told research staff that Opus 4.5 and 4.6 give them roughly a 2-3x speedup on internal research, suggesting AI-on-AI compounding is now a measurable driver of the trend.

For learners: benchmarks that look exponential on a log chart are the ones worth watching, but they are also the ones most likely to be gamed, saturated, or misread. The right instinct when you see 'AI doubling every four months' is to ask what, exactly, is being measured — and whether the ruler is still calibrated. METR is unusually honest about its own uncertainty; most capability charts shared on social media are not.
